analysis.one_liner: Requires most employers with 15 or more workers to provide at least seven paid sick days a year.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it sat in the Senate's labor committee from June 2004 until the Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The Healthy Families Act would have required every employer with 15 or more employees to give workers at least seven paid sick days a year, with a smaller pro-rated amount for part-timers. Workers could use the days for their own illness or medical care, or to care for a child, spouse, parent, or other close family member. Employers that already offered equivalent paid leave would not have to change anything, and could not cut existing leave to comply.
analysis.who_benefits: Millions of workers who have no paid sick leave, especially low-wage workers. The bill's own findings state that 76 percent of the poorest families lack regular paid sick leave, and fewer than half of workers who have paid leave can use it to care for a sick child. Workers would gain guaranteed paid time for their own medical care and to care for family members, without risking their pay or their job.

how_it_helps.text: Requires employers with 15 or more employees to provide at least seven days of paid sick leave annually to full-time workers, and a pro-rated amount to part-timers working at least 20 hours a week or 1,000 hours a year.

Workers may use the leave for their own illness, injury, or medical care, including preventive care and diagnostic visits, and to care for a child, spouse, parent, or others in a family-like relationship.

The bill protects workers from retaliation: employers may not fire or discriminate against anyone for using or requesting the leave or for filing a complaint, and workers can sue for lost wages and liquidated damages.
Employers with existing paid leave policies that are at least as generous do not have to change them, and no employer may reduce leave that already exists in order to comply.

The bill's findings cite evidence that the absence of sick leave falls hardest on low-income families — 76 percent of the poorest families lack regular paid sick leave — and that women bear most caregiving duties, so a gender-neutral leave standard reduces the burden and the risk of discrimination.

analysis.who_pays: Covered employers — private businesses and government offices with 15 or more employees — bear the cost of the paid leave itself, plus recordkeeping and compliance. Businesses with 14 or fewer employees are exempt.

drawbacks.text: The leave is a real cost to employers: seven paid days per full-time worker is roughly 2.7 percent of annual payroll, a burden that falls on small businesses at the 15-employee threshold and on low-margin industries that currently offer little or no paid leave.

The bill adds federal paperwork and enforcement — recordkeeping under the Fair Labor Standards Act regime, posting requirements with fines for willful violations, and possible employee lawsuits with attorney's fees — which honest supporters would acknowledge creates compliance friction, particularly for firms with variable-schedule workforces.

Critics of mandated sick leave generally argue that employers respond to benefit mandates by cutting wages or hiring, and the bill itself requires a Government Accountability Office study of the costs to employers and effects on retention, an acknowledgment that the cost side needed measuring.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the benefit is concrete and universal within the covered workforce: guaranteed paid time when they or a family member are sick, something a large share of low-income workers had none of. For employers, the cost is real but modest per worker, and the bill is carefully built to limit friction — a 15-employee floor, equivalency for existing generous policies, a ban on stripping existing leave, a 3-day doctor's note threshold, and a scheduling obligation on workers not to unduly disrupt operations. The design is more moderate than most benefit mandates; the main honest cost is the payroll expense on small and low-margin employers.

outcome.mechanism: Senator Kennedy introduced it in June 2004 and it went straight to the Senate committee that handles labor bills, which never took it up; the bill died there when the 108th Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Senator Edward Kennedy and seven cosponsors introduced the Healthy Families Act in the Senate on June 15, 2004.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No further action appears in the record — no hearing, no markup, no committee or floor vote — and the Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers with 15 or more employees who would have owed seven paid sick days per worker are better off, since no mandate was enacted. Workers without paid sick leave gained nothing and would wait years for federal action.

for.name: Sen. Edward Kennedy
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Healthy Families Act to create a federal paid sick leave mandate.

for.name: 8 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as original co-sponsors at introduction.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee leadership
against.role: Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on June 15, 2004 and took no recorded action on it for the rest of the Congress — no hearing, no markup, no vote.

against.name: Senate Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Held the Senate majority through the end of the 108th Congress and never brought the bill to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat — Senator Kennedy plus 8 Democratic cosponsors — and no Republican support appears in the record [S4].

industries.industry: Employers with 15 or more employees (retail, food service, and other low-benefit industries especially)
industries.note: The bill would have required these employers to pay for at least seven sick days per full-time worker per year and to keep records proving compliance. The cost falls hardest on industries that currently offer little or no paid leave, which is precisely where most workers without sick leave are.

industries.industry: Small employers with fewer than 15 employees
industries.note: They were exempt from the mandate, avoiding the payroll cost their larger competitors would have carried. In industries where small and large firms compete for the same workers, the exemption could also make it marginally easier for small firms to hire.
